newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Gunfire heard in Albania port as troops arrive.
newsitem.headline: Gunfire heard in Albania port as troops arrive.

text.p: Regular bursts of gunfire crackled in the southern Albanian port city of Vlore on Thursday as Italian marines, part of a multinational force mandated to protect aid shipments to the chaotic Balkan state, took up guard duty at dockside.

A carload of Albanian gunmen drove straight up to the small advance force of about 25 men and their leader, wearing a bullet-proof vest and carrying a Kalashnikov assault rifle, welcomed them to his hometown.
"You are my brothers," the man said.
"Welcome. If you need any help, you can ask me," he added.
Residents said the gunman was a well-known drug smuggler. He said he was a friend of the rebel committee which runs the city.
The Italians, the first troops of the United Nations-sanctioned multinational force to reach the south, were polite but reserved with the gang who sped off after the brief greeting.
They were left to patrol the pier and to prepare for a landing of at least 100 Greek troops due to arrive in the northern port of Durres on Friday and to travel on to Vlore later.
The regular automatic weapons fire and two loud explosions were heard in the city itself. The Italian marines had arrived earlier in the day from the capital Tirana to secure the Adriatic port.
The soldiers are part of the Italian-led mission which is fanning out across Albania to protect humanitarian aid convoys.
Soldiers said they did not know when the first aid shipment would reach Vlore.
Residents said nearly everyone in Vlore, as in many other parts of Albania, was armed. One man showed a reporter a grenade he kept in his pocket.
Albanians looted arsenals during an uprising earlier this year that erupted after the failure of get-rich-quick investment schemes in which many had invested their life savings.

Dozens of dock workers and local people crowded in front of the Italian green armoured personnel carriers at Vlore pier. One soldier stood above them, shielded by a wall, and stared through his rifle sights into the distance.
An Italian minesweeper was slowly criss-crossed the harbour in front of the pier searching for underwater devices.
"All the people of this city are delighted to welcome the Italian troops," said Abedin Nebiu, a 47-year-old veterinarian.

The Italian soldiers said they did not fear the violence in Albania. "I am not worried. Don't worry, be happy," said Alessandro, a private who declined to give his last name. Children swarmed around the soldiers, many of whom had added dark glasses to their full combat gear in the sunshine. The Italians were polite and unthreatening.
Another soldier, Salvatore, said: "Our priority now is to set up camp and check the road".
Along the main coastal route, gangs of men in civilian dress with guns rode in four wheeled drive vehicles. Two burned-out cars were used as a barricades for a makeshift checkpoint.
